title: Winter Games
build: Epyx original, PAL, two disk sides (C64 Preservation Project, verified dump)

records.c: File M's entry, where the loader starts the menu after every load of it and after RUN/STOP and RESTORE. It marks the menu as in memory ($083D = 0), silences the SID (music_init), sets up the text screen, makes CIA 1's port A all outputs and port B all inputs for the keyboard, and then either resumes where the menu left off to load an event (the address at $085D-$085E, kept by run_file) or starts at the main menu.

The main menu: sets the resume address back to here, draws the seven options with the number of joysticks as option 5's digit (the inline string's byte at $0F88), and, when $087F is set, "YES)" on option 6's line. Then the pointer chooses (choose_option, starting at the last choice, kept in $083E) and the RTS table main_menu_lo/main_menu_hi runs the option.

The main menu's text for print_inline: screen address $04CD, then the seven options, each line placed with code 1 and built from shared words with code 2: "1) COMPETE IN ALL THE EVENTS" to "7) OPENING CEREMONIES".
The digit of "NUMBER OF JOYSTICKS: 2" inside main_menu's inline string, which main_menu writes from $087D before printing it.
After the options: "YES)" on option 6's line when $087F is set.
"YES)" at screen address $0677, on option 6's line, printed when $087F is set: what is left of a line for the switch opt_more_events turns over.
Seven options (A = 6), from the last one chosen, the pointer's top at line $56; the option's routine is entered through the RTS table.

The low bytes, less one, of the eight option routines for the RTS at $0FCC: all events, some events, one event, practice, joysticks, world records, opening ceremony, and an eighth that only returns to main_menu.
The high bytes of the option routines.
Option 7: loads and runs file 1, the opening ceremony (run_file). The ceremony's exit through the loader brings the menu back to the main menu.
The eighth entry of the option table: back to main_menu. choose_option never returns it here, as main_menu offers seven.
Option 5: switches the number of joysticks at $087D between 1 and 2.

Turns $087F over between 0 and $FF, the switch that offers sixteen events instead of seven: the nine of event_names after Bobsled are Summer Games events. Nothing jumps here, so the switch stays 0 (loader_boot clears it); set by hand, the main menu shows "YES)" on option 6's line and the event lists run to SKEET SHOOTING.

Option 4: practice. One player (count $081E = 1) named "CONTESTANT" ($081D = $FF says so), the event chosen from the list, its scores cleared, and the event run; when the menu comes back it clears the player count and the flag and returns to the main menu.

Option 3: one event in competition: the players (check_players), "COMPETE IN WHICH EVENT?", the order of play shuffled, scores cleared, the event chosen and run; when the menu comes back, its results (show_results), then the main menu.
"COMPETE IN WHICH EVENT?" at $04A3; practice_screen prints its second half, "WHICH EVENT?", from $104D.
The order of play shuffled, the scores cleared, the event chosen and run; its results when the menu comes back.
Option 1: all seven events. The players (check_players), every event's bit set in $089D-$089E, then compete.

Runs a competition over the events whose bits are set in $089D-$089E: first the opening ceremony (file 1), then, from the menu's next start here, each chosen event in turn with its results, the medal table between events and a new order of play for each; at the end the final standings, the winner's flag and anthem. With $087F clear only the first seven bits count.
"FINAL STANDINGS:" at $05E3.
The final standings' tune (country slot 6), then each place from the last to the first with its pause, and the winner's flag and anthem.
The first pause of the final standings, in units of 74 frames (pause_music), by the number of players less one: 7, 3, 3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 0.
The pauses between the next places, read at $1114 plus the number of players: 8, 4, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1 for one to eight. Its first byte is also the last of standings_wait_first.
Waits for the controls to be let go (wait_released), then up to twice A frames, or until fire.
Waits A times 74 frames, stepping the tune twice a frame.

Option 2: the players (check_players), then "SELECT THE EVENTS TO COMPETE IN": the events listed in black and DONE in blue; choosing an event turns it white and sets its bit in $089D-$089E (event_bits_hi, event_bits_lo), choosing it again turns it back. DONE with any chosen starts compete, with none the main menu.
"SELECT THE EVENTS TO COMPETE IN" at $04A3.
No events chosen yet; the list in black and DONE in blue.
"DONE" at $0725, under the list of events.
The choosing loop: the pointer over the events and DONE, an event's colour and bit turned over each time it is chosen.
The bit in $089D for each event 0-15: $80 to $01 for the first eight, then 0.
The bit in $089E for each event 0-15: 0 for the first eight, then $80 to $01. The two tables share their eight zeros.

Option 6: the world records, "WORLD RECORDS:" and under it each event's name, its record holder and score from the records at $0E00 (show_record_name, show_record_score), with tune 38 played over and over until fire is pressed.
"WORLD RECORDS:" at $04A3.
The records screen's lines, one an event: name, colon, the spaces of record_gaps, the holder's name and score; then tune 38 until fire.

Keeps the return address on the stack, the option's call of check_players, as the menu's resume address and runs name_entry; name entry ends through the loader's restart, which starts the menu again there, back in the option.
"NEXT EVENT:" and the event's name, then a wait of up to 400 frames or until fire (wait_or_fire with 200).
"NEXT EVENT:" at $04A3.
The event's name, then the wait.
show_next_event, then loads and runs the event: file number $081F + 4 (run_file).
Loads and runs file X through the loader's $0903, first keeping the caller's return address plus one at $085D-$085E, where the menu resumes when it starts again after the file has run.
Prints the string that follows the JSR: a screen address, then text for print_text; returns past the string's closing 0.
Reads the next byte of text at ($2C) and moves the pointer on; Z is set for a 0.
Moves the text pointer ($2C) on by one without reading.
Prints a space, keeping A.
Prints A in colour Y. Nothing calls it here; print_bullet enters past its first instruction.
Prints A in the colour in Y, which becomes the colour for what follows.
Puts A on the screen at ($2E) and the colour in $46 at the same place in colour RAM (the screen's high byte EOR $DC: $04-$07 become $D8-$DB), and moves on.
Prints the bullet, character $D4, in red, before a player's name.

The menu's screen: black border, cyan background, blue as the multicolour, text multicolour from the character set at $2000, every cell blank in cyan; a top and a bottom row of characters $B9 and $BA, and the red and white dashed line across row 2.
Prints the name of the record holder of event $081F, 10 characters from the record at $0E00 (record_offsets).
Prints X characters from the address A (high) and Y (low).
Prints the name of event $081F (event_names).
Prints the name of event X.
Prints the string at A (high) and Y (low); give_medal enters here for the medal's name.
The control codes of print_text: 1 and two bytes, a new screen address; 2 and two bytes, the string at that address, printed and returned from; any other byte is a character.
Prints the string at X (low) and Y (high).
Prints the string at ($2C) until its 0, with print_code's codes: the menu's texts share their common words (") COMPETE IN ", " EVENT", "WORLD RECORD") through code 2.
Where each event's world record starts at $0E00: 20 bytes each, 0 to $8C, for eight events.
Prints event $081F's record score, 6 characters from offset 11 of its record.
Between events: the totals worked out and sorted, and "COMPETITOR G S B TOTAL" with every player's medals and points.
"COMPETITOR G S B TOTAL" at $051B, the medal table's heading.
A row of the medal table for each player: bullet, name, country, the three medal counts and the points.
Prints player $37's bullet, name and country, 16 characters of the record (player_offsets).
Two spaces and the 6 characters of a player's score text.
Prints the player's gold, silver and bronze counts and points total (record offsets $19-$1B and $16).
Each player's points from the medals, 5 for gold, 3 for silver and 1 for bronze, into offset $16 of the record, where sort_players finds it.
Three spaces and a two-digit number.
Prints A (below 100) as two digits, a space in place of a leading 0.
Gives player Y the medal of place $3A when the player's score is not 0 and the place is in the first three: one more at offset $19 + place, and "GOLD", "SILVER" or "BRONZE" printed beside the score.
The low bytes of "GOLD", "SILVER" and "BRONZE".
Their high bytes.
"PRACTICE WHICH EVENT?" (the second half of the words from opt_one_event's string, at $104D), then choose_event.
"PRACTICE WHICH EVENT?" at $04A3, two shared strings.
Lists the events and lets the pointer choose; the event is kept in $083F and $081F.
Prints every event the menu offers (list_event), A) to G), or to P) with $087F set.
Prints event $39 as a letter and its name, on every second row, or every row when sixteen are listed.
"CONTESTANT" and six spaces, the name opt_practice gives all eight players.
Before a competition: clears the medals; with players already named it asks "IS THIS CORRECT?" and goes on for YES. Otherwise, or for NO, it enters the names (to_name_entry).
"IS THIS CORRECT?", "A) YES", "B) NO" and every player's name and country; returns the choice (0 for yes).
"IS THIS CORRECT?" at $04CB.
"A) YES".
"A) YES" at $051D.
"B) NO".
"B) NO" at $056D.
Every player's name and country under the question, then the pointer on YES and NO.
Clears every player's medal counts (offsets $19-$1B of the eight records).
Clears every player's score (offsets $16-$18) and score text (six spaces at $10-$15).
The low bytes of the sixteen events' names.
Their high bytes, all $16.

The sixteen events' names as print_text strings: Ski Jump, Hot Dog, Biathlon, Bobsled, Free Skating, Figure Skating, Speed Skating, then Cycling, Pole Vault, Platform Diving, 4 x 400 m Relay, 100 m Dash, Gymnastics, Freestyle Relay, 100 m Freestyle and Skeet Shooting, the events of Epyx's Summer Games and Summer Games II, which only opt_more_events would offer.
"WORLD RECORD", whose last seven characters, " RECORD", are a string of their own.
The spaces after each event's name on the records screen, to line the holders up.
"GOLD", "SILVER" and "BRONZE".
") COMPETE IN ", a string the menu's texts share, as are its last eleven characters.
"ONE EVENT", whose last six characters " EVENT" are shared too.
"ING CEREMONIES", for "OPENING CEREMONIES".
"PRACTICE ".

An event's results: the players sorted by score, scores of 0 shown as FAULT, the world record checked, "CONTESTANTS SCORE" with each place (players with the same score share it) and the medals; then the winner's flag and anthem, until fire.
"CONTESTANTS SCORE" at $060B, the results' heading.
A row for each player: the place (players with the same score as the one above share it), name, country, score and medal.
Shows the winning country's flag ($081C of the first record) on its white band and plays its anthem, then waits for fire.
One frame of the flag on show: the background white from raster line $4D and cyan again from $8D, the tune stepped twice; it returns once the tune has ended and $16 more frames have passed.
Compares player X's score with the next player's; Z set when they are equal.
For each player: a score text ending in M gets the small m (character $B8), and a score of 0 becomes " FAULT".

When the winner's score beats event $081F's world record, prints the old and new records, copies the winner's name and score into the record at $0E00, waits up to 200 frames or for fire and saves the records to the disk through the loader's $0934. Only the first eight events have records.
"NEW WORLD RECORD FOR" the event, "OLD RECORD:" and the old holder and score, "NEW RECORD:".
"NEW WORLD RECORD FOR" at $04CB.
The event's name, then the old record's line.
"OLD RECORD:" at $051B.
The old holder's name and score, then "NEW RECORD:".
"NEW RECORD:" at $056B.
Returns; check_record prints the new holder's name and score after it.
Draws flag Y on the results screen, ten characters by five rows from the flags' strip (flag_screen_lo and _hi, flag_colour_lo and _hi), with its two shared colours from flag_mc.
Copies five rows of ten bytes from ($2C), a row of the strip (78 bytes) apart, to ($2E), a screen row apart.
For each country (row times 8 plus column of the chooser, 0-21), the low byte of its flag in the strip's characters; slots 6, 7, 14 and 15 are 0.
The high bytes of the flags' characters.
The low bytes of the flags' colours in the strip.
The high bytes of the flags' colours in the strip.
Each flag's two multicolour colours, the low nybble for $D022, the high for $D023.
Sorts the player records by score (offsets $16-$18), highest first, swapping whole records.
Puts the players in a random order: each record swapped with a random one (random_player).
Swaps the player records at $0800+X and $0800+Y, up to offset $1C, leaving the three bytes of shared variables at the end of each alone.
The swap's RTS; player_order is read from one byte before player_offsets.

Each player's record in the page at $0800: 32 bytes each, 0 to $E0. Bytes $00-$0A of a record are the name, $0B-$0F the country code in brackets, $10-$15 the score as text, $16-$18 the score, $19-$1B the medals, $1C the country; $1D-$1F are not the player's but the game's shared variables ($081D-$081F, $083D-$083F and so on).
A random number below the number of players.
Steps the random number at $08FD-$08FE and the counter at $08FF, and returns the two mixed. wait_frame calls it every frame, so time spent waiting stirs it.
The pointer on "A) YES" and "B) NO".
The pointer on a list starting at screen line $5E (choose_option).

Lets the player choose one of A+1 options with a pointer sprite, from option X, the pointer's top at line Y: up and down on either joystick move it, holding repeats every 24 frames, fire chooses; or a digit or letter key chooses at once (1 or A for the first). Lists of eleven options or more are single-spaced. Returns the choice in X.
Waits until neither fire nor a key has been held for 15 frames in a row.
Puts the pointer, sprite 0 (shape $C3) in blue, at option $30.
Waits for the controls to be let go, then for fire. Nothing calls it here.
Screen offsets of the event list, every second row: low bytes.
The high bytes of the every-second-row offsets.
Screen offsets for one row each, for sixteen events or eight players: low bytes.
The high bytes of the one-a-row screen offsets.

Waits for raster line 250 and then 251, a frame; stirs random; reads both joysticks (port A AND port B, the low five bits) and keeps a reading that holds for two frames in $36. Returns the fire bit, 0 when pressed.
Waits for raster line A.
Denmark's anthem, tune 34: records of four bytes, three notes and a length, to an end mark (bit 7). All the tunes below are in this form, played by music_step.
France's anthem, tune 2.
The U.S.A.'s anthem, tune 0, also played for the four empty country slots.
Great Britain's anthem, tune 4. Its end mark at $1D32 is where music_init points the player.
The SID frequencies of 44 notes, low bytes: 0 for silence, then C sharp 2 up to G sharp 5, the opening's table, exact for an NTSC machine and two-thirds of a semitone flat on a PAL one.
The high bytes of the 44 notes' frequencies.
The note lengths in calls of music_step, by a note's fourth byte.
Silences the SID and sets every voice up: attack 2, decay 1, sustain 8, release 4, pulse width $400, volume 10; no tune playing ($12 = $FF, the pointer $10-$11 at an end mark).
Starts the tune of country slot Y (tune_of_country) unless a tune with a lower number is playing.
The tune of each country slot, an offset into tunes: the eighteen anthems, with slot 6 for the final standings (36), slot 7 for the world records (38), and 0 (the U.S.A.'s) for the four empty slots.

The anthem player, the opening's design (two calls a frame; four bytes a note: three notes and a length): the gates go off for a note's last four calls; a new note sets each voice's test bit for a moment, then gates voices 1 and 2 on pulse and voice 3 on sawtooth.
Silences the three voices and marks no tune playing.
Spain's anthem, tune 24.
Norway's anthem, tune 30.
35 zero bytes, before the character set.

The menu's character set, where $D018 = $18 points the video chip, used in multicolour text: $20-$5F hold the digits, the letters and a few signs, with some pieces of flags among them, and most of 0-$1F and $60-$D4 are pieces of the flags and the screen's borders. Characters from $D5 up would lie on the flags' strip and are not used.
The character set from $80, flag pieces, to $D4 at $26A7.

The flags' strip, a picture 78 columns wide that the chooser scrolls through 40 at a time: six flags in each of three bands, 13 columns a flag. Here the first band, five rows of characters and then the row of names: U.S.A., France, Great Britain, West Germany, Austria and Italy.
The flags' strip, band 1, row 2 of the flags' characters, 78 columns.
The flags' strip, band 1, row 3 of the flags' characters, 78 columns.

The flags' strip, band 1: the row of names under the flags (U.S.A., France, Great Britain, West Germany, Austria and Italy).
The second band's characters: U.S.S.R., Canada, Mexico, Spain, Denmark and Australia.

The flags' strip, band 3: the row of names under the flags (Japan, the Netherlands, Epyx, Norway, Ireland and Brazil).
The colours of the first band's five rows of flags, for colour RAM.
The colours of band 1's row 2 of flags, 78 columns.

Ten zero bytes after the strip.
Sprite shape $C3: the pointer, a small triangle, that choose_option moves down the lists.
Sprite shape $C4: the frame's top left corner.
Shape $C5: the frame's top right corner.
Shape $C6: the frame's bottom left corner.
Shape $C7: the frame's bottom right corner.
Shape $C8: the arrow pointing right on the top line.
Shape $C9: the arrow pointing left.
The twenty tunes' addresses, by tune number (an even offset): the eighteen anthems, 36 for the final standings and 38 for the world records.
The tunes' addresses' high bytes, read at $3281 + the tune number.
Ireland's anthem, tune 32.
Epyx's anthem, tune 28, for the players who choose the company's flag.
Tune 38, which plays while the world records are shown, the longest of them, 86 notes.
Brazil's anthem, tune 26.
West Germany's anthem, tune 14.
Australia's anthem, tune 16.
Japan's anthem, tune 12.
The U.S.S.R.'s anthem, tune 6.
Canada's anthem, tune 8.
Mexico's anthem, tune 10.
Tune 36, for the final standings.
The Netherlands' anthem, tune 18.
Austria's anthem, tune 20.
Italy's anthem, tune 22.

The players' names and countries, a program of its own within the menu: zero page $11-$49 cleared, the flag chooser's screen and sprites, its raster interrupts, then a loop once a frame: the visible part of the flags' strip redrawn, the frame's colours and the fire and S keys, the step of the entry (entry_state), the joystick. It ends through the loader's $0900, which starts the menu again where to_name_entry left it.

Sprites 0-5 on, hires, 0-3 doubled both ways: the four corners of the frame round a flag (shapes $C4-$C7) and the two arrows (shapes $C8 and $C9), at the places in entry_sprite_pos; the corners start black, and entry_fire cycles all six's colours.
The six sprites' positions, X and Y for each of eight, and the high bits of X ($20, sprite 5).
The six sprites' shapes, $C4-$C9.
Turns the timer interrupts off and the raster interrupt on at line 251, with the KERNAL's IRQ vector ($0314) at entry_irq.

The name entry's raster interrupt, eight a frame: each runs the handler for the band of the screen it starts (entry_irq_lo and _hi, through an RTS) and sets the line of the next from entry_irq_lines. The handlers colour the backgrounds behind each band of flags, white behind a flag and black between, set the band's shared colours, count the frames at $14-$15 with a flag at $18 for the main loop, and step the anthem.
The raster lines of the eight interrupts, taken from the last: 251, 235, 192, 171, 128, 120, 108, 64.
The handlers' high bytes, all $3A.
The handlers' low bytes less one, for the RTS.
A handler: a step of the anthem.
Every handler's end: border black, the raster interrupt acknowledged, the registers restored.
A handler: white background, blue and red as the shared colours, behind the first band of flags.
A handler: black background between the bands.
A handler: white background, yellow as the first shared colour, behind the second band.
A handler: white background, light blue and yellow, behind the third band.
A handler: the frame count at $14-$15 and its flag at $18 for name_entry's loop, and a step of the anthem.
Clears zero page $11-$49.
Scans the keyboard: the code of the first key found held, from key_codes, in $23 and A; $FF when none is.
The values for CIA 1's port A that select each of the keyboard matrix's eight columns.
The bit of each of the matrix's eight rows in port B.
The character for each key, eight a column: digits and letters as ASCII, $0D for RETURN, $08 for DEL and for the cursor-right key, space as $20, $FF for the keys the entry has no use for.
Reads the keyboard row for column A, and returns $FF (nothing) when port B shows something with no column selected, a joystick in port 1 being held.

The name entry's steps, in $22: 0, no players yet; 1, a name prompt "#n ENTER YOUR NAME" with the arrows; 2, typing; 3, "PICK YOUR COUNTRY" with the frame round a flag; 4, choosing; 5 and over, "IS THIS CORRECT?", which goes to the loader's $0900 for YES and starts the entry again for NO.
An RTS nothing reaches.

Step 2: the name typed into row 0 from column 23, up to ten characters. A key acts when it changes (the same key held does not repeat); DEL takes the last character off; RETURN ends the name (name_done).

RETURN: a name the same as an earlier player's is refused; otherwise it is copied into the player's record. An empty name ends the list once there is a player (step 5), and is refused for the first; any other goes on to the country (step 3).
Leaves its caller (two return addresses dropped) when the typed name matches an earlier player's.
Step 3: the top line from pick_line with the player's name over its placeholder, the frame's four sprites on.
The top line while a country is chosen, 40 characters: "PICK YOUR COUNTRY" to the right, and at the left the placeholder "NELSON S.", which show_pick_line always covers with the player's name.

The three-letter codes of the 24 country slots, the chooser's three rows of eight: USA FRA GBR FRG AUT ITA, URS CAN MEX ESP DEN AUS, JPN HOL EPX NOR IRL BRA, with XXX in the last two of each row, which the chooser never reaches.
The second letter of each country code, read at $3CD2 + 3 times the country.
The third letters, read at $3CD3 + 3 times the country.

Step 4: a joystick moved while the frame is still, and before a country is chosen, starts a move of 28 frames: left or right scrolls the flags' strip one flag (13 columns) round, up or down moves the frame one band, within the three. Either stops the anthem.
The column step for each joystick reading (the low four bits): -1 for left, +1 for right.
The frame's step in lines for each reading: -4 for up, +4 for down.
One column of the move: the strip's first column visible ($1F) on by -1 or +1, round its 78.
Moves the frame's four sprites up or down by $1D lines.
Draws the 40 visible columns of the flags' strip, the last of them column $1F, wrapping round its 78: three bands of five rows of characters and colours and a row of names under each.

Each frame: the frame's colours cycled (frame_colours). In step 4, while an anthem plays nothing else happens; after a choice, the next player (step 1, or 5 after the eighth). Otherwise S plays the anthem of the flag in the frame, and fire chooses that country and plays its anthem too.
The frame's colours in turn, 0, 11, 12, 15, 1, 15, 12, 11: black through the greys to white and back.
The country under the frame (row times 8 plus column) into the player's record at offset $1C, and its code in brackets at $0B-$0F; returns it in Y for music_start.
The chooser's screen: the strip drawn from column 40, the frame on the second flag of the first band.
The colours of the rows and the lines between the bands (characters $5E and $5F), the top line from entry_top_line with the player's number.
"#1 ENTER YOUR NAME" with the arrows' places, 40 characters.
The file's last three bytes, after entry_top_line, which nothing reads.
